newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.

text.p: FULL SCALE SEARCH RESUMES FOR FIVE MISSING IN CORAL SEA
Authorities remain hopeful five people missing in the Coral Sea in rough conditions, will be found alive, despite believing their yacht has sunk.
A full scale search has resumed for the crew of the missing New Zealand yacht -- the Queen Charlotte.
Overnight ships used moonlight to search the area, near where debris and lifejackets were found yesterday.
Search co-ordinator Mike Jackson-Calway says it seems certain the yacht has sunk.
Four aircraft rejoined the search at first light and are now concentrating on finding a second emergency positioning beacon, which was pinpointed yesterday.
Authorities hope the beacon is coming from a life-raft.
JUSTIN STILL EDGING CLOSER TO COAST
A Tropical Cyclone warning has been issued for the coastal communities of north Queensland between Cooktown and Cardwell as Justin moves closer to the coast.
It's a Category one, the lowest on the scale, with maximum wind gusts up to 120 kilometers an hour.
Justin is currently moving in a west-south-westerly direction at 16 kilometres an hour.
It's about 360 kilometres east of Cooktown and 480 kilometres north northeast of Townsville.
The Weather Bureau expects Justin to take a more southerly course later today.
AD RACIST - CLAIM LABOR, DEMOCRATS AND ABORIGINAL LEADERS
The Federal Opposition, Australian Democrats and Aboriginal leaders have branded a television advertisement, which calls for the extinguishment of native title, as racist.

Funded by the National Farmers Federation, the one-week saturation ad features an Aboriginal boy playing a game of twister with a white boy, where they reach for black and white circles on the ground.
The Aborigine is depicted as winning the game.
Labor's spokesman on Aboriginal Affairs, Daryl Melham, says the ad pits black against white and completely misrepresents the High Court's Wik decision.
SENATE DEBATE ON ANDREWS BILL OVER
Senate debate on the Andrews anti-euthanasia bill ended last night leaving Senators the weekend to decide how they'll vote on the bill on Monday night.
The private members bill, put forward by Independent Senator Kevin Andrews, aims to override the Northern Territory's voluntary euthanasia law.
Fifty-nine members of the Upper House spoke during the course of the debate, with 30 declaring their intention to support the bill.
Sixteen senators didn't speak on the bill, and their votes will be crucial on Monday night.
The bill needs 37 votes to pass the Senate.
PREMIERS CONFERENCE IN CANBERRA TODAY
The Federal Government is describing as reasonable the financial offer it'll be making to the States and Territories at today's Premiers Conference in Canberra.
The Premiers and Chief Ministers fear the Commonwealth will make further cuts to specific purporse payments for health, education and housing, as it searches for ways to reduce the budget deficit.
Last year, the Federal Government cut these payments by two per-cent, and some states fear the three-billion dollar deficit blow-out will result in even bigger cuts this year.
The Prime Minister won't disclose what the Commonwealth's planning to do, only that it's latest offer is reasonable.

Mr Howard has also indicated there'll be no changes to last year's deal that will see the States and Territories forego one-and-a-half-billion dollars in general financial assistance grants over three years.
The Prime Minister hosted a dinner for the State and Territory leaders last night at The Lodge, during which they discussed native title issues.
ACCOUNTANTS SLAM SUPER SURCHARGE
The Federal Government's planned 15 percent superannuation surcharge on high income earners has attracted further criticism, this time from accountants.
Coopers and Lybrand's Gabriel Szondy says the plan's already having an impact with people holding back putting money into super funds because of uncertainty about the industry's future.
Mr Szondy says if high income earners decide to only contribute the Super Guarantee amount, the Government won't get its expected revenue of 500-million dollars from the scheme.
He also says the scheme's unfair, and too costly and complex for super funds to administer.
